newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat needs political gains, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Arafat needs political gains, analysts say.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has to find a way of capitalising on last week's Arab-Israeli violence as the crisis returns to diplomatic arena this week, political analysts said.
But the Israeli government, which sent tanks to the edges of the West Bank and Gaza, vowed that he would reap no political gains from the gun battles which it says he instigated.

U.S. President Bill Clinton has invited Arafat, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Jordan's King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to talks in Washington to try to defuse the situation and restart peace negotiations.

Arafat was due to go to Egypt on Monday to try to persuade Mubarak, who has criticised Israel over the slow pace of peace-making, to attend the summit, tentatively scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Marwan Kanafani, an Arafat spokesman, said the Palestinian leader had to show his people that the Arabs killed in clashes with Israeli forces last week had not died in vain.

"Arafat cannot ignore the fact there are about 60 Palestinian martyrs," Kanafani said. "The Washington summit has to be a successful meeting with concrete results on advancing peace and implementing peace deals."
Political analyst Khalil al-Shikaki said that, with frustration building up among Palestinians, Arafat had no choice but confrontation.
"But he has a dilemma because, if demonstrations continue, he might lose control and, if he tries to rein it in quickly, he might not be able to capitalise on it," Shikaki said.

The Palestinians insist that Israel must close the tourist-archaeological tunnel whose opening in Arab East Jerusalem triggered the violence and start implementing self-rule deals, including a partial troop pullout from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"If these issues are not solved soon, Arafat has no option but to escalate in response and the whole peace process will collapse and the whole region will flare up in flames," said U.N. envoy Terje Larsen who is trying to mediate in the crisis.

Netanyahu has rejected calls to close the tunnel, reopened on Sunday after a two-day break for the Jewish Sabbath. Citing security concerns, he also says the Hebron redeployment accord must be modified to protect Jewish settlers more effectively.

"The question is: If Netanyahu persists in his intransigence, will Arafat adopt a confrontational line or the wait-and-see approach which he tried and proved a failure," Shikaki said. "Of course the only option is confrontation."

Only months ago, Arafat risked popular support in the West Bank and Gaza by ordering his 30,000-man paramilitary forces to crack down on Islamic militant groups trying to sabotage the peace process by carrying out suicide bombings in Israel.
This time, he restored his credibility among many Palestininans by allowing his forces to shoot at Israeli soldiers during clashes in which rock-throwing Arabs were wounded by Israeli gunfire.
